**(A) yes**

I think a pregnant woman should be able to make that decision for herself. It's her body and her life circumstances, and she's in the best position to know what's right for her situation. I'd rather that decision stay between her and her doctor than have the government involved in something that personal.

**(A) yes**

That's an incredibly difficult situation, and it feels right that she — along with her doctor and family — should be the one making that call, not the government. No one should be forced into that circumstance without a choice.

**(A) yes**

If a woman's health is seriously at risk, she should absolutely have access to a legal abortion. That seems like a pretty straightforward medical necessity to me — you can't ignore a serious threat to someone's life or health. I think most reasonable people, regardless of where they stand on the broader abortion debate, would agree that protecting the mother's health in a dangerous situation has to be a priority.

**(A) yes**

Honestly, I think a woman's circumstances — including being married and feeling her family is complete — are valid reasons. It's her body and her life. I don't think being married changes the fundamental right to make that decision for yourself.

**(A) yes**

Financial hardship is a real and significant factor in people's lives. If a family genuinely cannot afford to raise another child, forcing them into that situation doesn't seem fair to the parents or to the child who would be born into poverty. People should have the ability to make decisions that are right for their actual circumstances.

**(A) yes**

Yes, I think in that situation a woman should be able to obtain a legal abortion. A pregnancy resulting from rape wasn't a choice she made, and forcing someone to carry that pregnancy to term feels like compounding an already terrible trauma. That seems like a situation where most people, even those who have reservations about abortion more broadly, would agree she should have that option available to her.

**(A) yes**

**(B) inspired word**

I think the Bible carries deep spiritual meaning and wisdom, but I also recognize it was written by human beings in specific historical and cultural contexts. Taking every passage completely literally seems to miss the point of a lot of it — there's poetry, metaphor, and allegory throughout. But dismissing it entirely as just an ancient collection of fables feels like it goes too far in the other direction. The middle ground makes the most sense to me.

**(B) oppose**

I think taking a life, even as punishment, puts the state in the position of doing the very thing we're condemning. There's also the reality that the justice system isn't perfect — innocent people have been executed. That's irreversible. Life imprisonment without parole accomplishes the same goal of keeping dangerous people off the streets without that finality.
**(C) middle class**

**(A) Yes, allowed to teach**

Someone's personal views on religion shouldn't disqualify them from teaching at a college or university. Academic freedom is pretty fundamental to higher education. What matters is whether they can do their job competently and professionally — teach the subject matter, engage students fairly, and not use the classroom as a platform to push their personal agenda inappropriately. Those same standards apply to religious believers too. Personal beliefs, whatever they are, shouldn't be a litmus test for employment.

**(A) a great deal**

The military is one of those institutions I tend to trust more than most. They have a clear mission, a strong culture of discipline and service, and there's something about the personal sacrifice involved that commands respect. I feel fairly confident in the people running it.

**(B) only some confidence**

Major companies can be innovative and create jobs, but their primary focus on profits sometimes puts them at odds with what's best for workers or communities. I've seen enough examples of corporate misconduct and prioritizing shareholders over everything else to not have a *great deal* of confidence — but I don't want to be entirely cynical either. Some companies do genuinely try to do right by their employees and customers. So "only some" feels about right.

**(B) only some**

I think there's genuine good being done by many religious organizations — community support, charity work, moral guidance for people who find meaning in it. But there's also been enough scandal, abuse cover-ups, and political maneuvering over the years that I can't say I have a *great deal* of confidence in the leadership. The people in the pews are often fine; it's the institutional leadership where my trust gets shaky.

**(B) only some confidence**

Education as a system still matters a lot to me, and there are dedicated teachers and administrators doing genuinely good work. But I have real concerns about whether the people running educational institutions — at the policy and administrative levels — are consistently making the right calls. There's a lot of bureaucracy, political pressure, and sometimes decisions that seem disconnected from what actually helps students learn. So "only some" feels honest — not cynical, but not fully confident either.

**(C) hardly any**

Honestly, it feels like the executive branch has been pretty unpredictable and polarizing for a while now. There's a lot of dysfunction, and it's hard to feel confident that decisions are being made with regular people in mind. I don't have a lot of faith in it right now.

**(B) only some**

Banks and financial institutions do provide essential services and there are regulatory frameworks in place, but there have been enough financial crises, scandals, and instances where institutions prioritized profits over customers to make full confidence hard to justify. I trust them enough to use them, but I stay cautious and keep an eye on things.

**(B) only some**

I think the Court has important work to do and I respect the institution itself, but some of the decisions and the way the confirmation process has become so politicized over the years... it's hard to have full confidence. I trust that the justices are generally knowledgeable and working within the law, but I'm not sure the institution is fully insulated from politics the way it's supposed to be. So "only some" feels about right for me.

**(B) only some confidence**

Organized labor has its place — fighting for workers' rights, fair wages, better conditions. That history matters and I respect it. But from what I've seen, some unions can be more focused on protecting their own bureaucracy or seniority systems than actually serving workers' best interests, and leadership doesn't always seem accountable to the members. So I'm somewhere in the middle — not dismissive of unions, but not fully confident in the people running them either.

**(C) hardly any**

Honestly, Congress just hasn't given me much reason to feel confident. It feels like there's a lot of gridlock, a lot of partisan fighting, and not a whole lot of getting things done for regular people. I follow the news enough to see that they struggle to agree on much of anything, and when they do pass something, it often feels like it's been watered down or loaded with stuff that benefits special interests. So yeah — hardly any confidence.

**(A) a great deal**

I have a great deal of confidence in medicine. The people running medical institutions — researchers, physicians, hospital administrators — are generally dedicated professionals working within rigorous scientific frameworks. Medical science has given us vaccines, treatments for once-fatal diseases, and continuously improving care. Are there problems with healthcare systems? Sure. But confidence in the institution of medicine itself? That's high for me.

**(C) hardly any**

Honestly, the press has made it pretty hard to trust them over the years. There's so much that feels like it's driven by clicks and engagement rather than just reporting what's happening. You see the same story spun completely differently depending on which outlet you're reading, and it makes you wonder who's actually trying to give you the straight picture. I don't think everyone in journalism is acting in bad faith, but as an institution? Hardly any confidence at this point.

**(A) a great deal**

I have a great deal of confidence in the scientific community. Scientists go through rigorous training, peer review keeps them accountable, and the overall process of science — testing, revising, building on evidence — has a pretty strong track record. Sure, individual studies can be flawed or overhyped, but the institution as a whole? I trust it.

**(C) hardly any**

Honestly, I've grown pretty skeptical of television news and media over the years. There's so much sensationalism, obvious bias depending on which channel you're watching, and it often feels like ratings and engagement drive coverage more than accuracy or public interest. I'll catch a story on TV and then look it up myself because I don't fully trust what I'm hearing. So yeah — hardly any confidence in the people running it.

**(B) not harshly enough**

Honestly, it often feels like sentences don't reflect the seriousness of the crimes. You hear about repeat offenders who keep cycling through the system, and it makes you wonder if the consequences are actually serving as a deterrent. I think most people in my community feel the same way — that there's a disconnect between what happens in the courtroom and what feels like justice.

**(C) stay as is**

Honestly, I think the current process strikes a reasonable balance. It's not so easy that people make impulsive decisions, but it's also not so burdensome that people feel trapped in genuinely unhealthy or harmful situations. Marriage is a serious commitment, but so is the ability to leave one when it's not working. I wouldn't want to tip too far in either direction.

**(C) depends**

Honestly, I think it really comes down to the situation and the person. Most people I encounter day-to-day seem decent and fair — they're not looking to exploit anyone. But put someone under financial pressure, or in a situation where they think they won't get caught, and the calculus can shift. I've seen both sides of it. So a blanket answer either way wouldn't feel honest to me.

**(A) strongly agree**

A mother's warmth and the security she provides her children really comes down to the quality of time and emotional connection, not the quantity of hours spent at home. Working mothers I've seen — including in my own life — are just as capable of forming deep, loving bonds with their kids. It's about presence, attention, and love when you're together, not whether you have a job.
(C) disagree

**(B) disagree**

I don't think emotional suitability for politics breaks down along gender lines. What makes someone effective in politics — things like empathy, resilience, decisiveness, communication — those traits vary by individual, not by gender. I've seen plenty of men who were emotionally ill-suited for leadership and plenty of women who were exceptional at it, and vice versa. The statement feels like an outdated generalization to me.
(C) disagree
**(C) average**

**(B) hard work, luck equally important**

Honestly, I think it's pretty naive to say it's all one or the other. I've seen hardworking people struggle for years while someone else catches a break at the right moment. But I've also seen lucky opportunities go nowhere because the person wasn't prepared or willing to put in the effort. 

It really seems like both play a role — hard work gets you ready and keeps you in the game, but luck or the right connections can open doors that hard work alone might never reach.

**(E) believe with doubts**

Yeah, that one fits me best. I believe in God, but I'd be lying if I said I never had questions or moments where I'm not sure. Life throws things at you that make you wonder. But at the end of the day, that belief is still there — just not without some uncertainty mixed in.

**(A) Should be legal**

I think it should be legal. At this point, so many states have already gone that route, and the evidence seems to show that legalization — when done with proper regulation — can be managed responsibly. Adults should generally be able to make their own choices, and keeping it illegal just seems to push it underground without really solving anything.

**(A) favor**

Yeah, I'd be in favor of that. Seems reasonable to me that there should be some kind of check before someone can just go out and buy a gun. A permit process means law enforcement has a chance to screen people — make sure someone doesn't have a violent history or something that would make it dangerous for them to have a firearm. It's not about taking guns away from people, just adding a layer of accountability. I can live with that.

**(B) pretty happy**

Things are going reasonably well overall. There are always ups and downs, but I'd say I'm in a decent place — not over the moon, but definitely not struggling either. Just kind of steady, you know? Life feels manageable and there's enough good stuff to feel grateful for.

**(B) good**

Pretty good overall, I'd say. Nothing major going on, a few minor things here and there that come with getting older, but I can't complain too much.

**(C) depends**

Honestly, I think it really varies depending on the situation and the person. In everyday interactions — like someone holding a door open or giving directions — most people do seem genuinely helpful. But when there are real stakes involved, like money, competition, or personal cost, self-interest tends to take over more often. I don't think people are fundamentally selfish *or* fundamentally altruistic — it's more situational than that.

**(D) not wrong at all**

Two consenting adults — whatever their gender — it's their business, not mine. I don't see any harm in it.

**(A) yes**

If someone is suffering from an incurable disease and both they and their family have made that difficult decision together, I think it's compassionate to allow doctors that option. People should have some agency over how they face the end of their lives, especially when there's no hope of recovery. It's not a decision anyone takes lightly.

**(B) not remove**

Even if someone's views on religion are pretty far out there or I personally disagree with them, I don't think a public library should pull a book just because people find the ideas offensive or uncomfortable. Libraries are supposed to be a place where all kinds of perspectives are available. If we start removing books every time a group objects to the content, where does that end? I'd rather let people make their own choices about what to read.

**(A) exciting**

Honestly, I'd say exciting. There's always something new coming up — whether it's big life changes or just small unexpected moments day to day. Even the routine parts of life have their own rhythm that I find kind of satisfying rather than boring. I think a lot of it comes down to perspective.

**(C) too much**

Honestly, with all the issues we have here at home — infrastructure, healthcare costs, people struggling to get by — it's hard to justify sending so much money overseas. I think we need to get our own house in order first. That's just my gut feeling on it.

**(C) too much**

Honestly, when I look at the defense budget compared to what we spend on things like infrastructure, healthcare, and education, it feels out of balance. We're already by far the biggest military spender in the world. I think we could trim some of that and redirect it toward problems that affect people's daily lives more directly.

**(A) too little**

Honestly, the infrastructure issues, housing costs, and homelessness you see in major cities don't seem like problems that are getting better on their own. I think we're underfunding the kinds of long-term investments — affordable housing, public transit, social services — that could actually make a dent. It feels like we put out fires reactively rather than addressing root causes with sustained funding.

**(A) too little**

Crime affects everyday life in real ways — safety in neighborhoods, people's ability to go about their day without worry. I think we could be doing more, whether that's investing in prevention programs, better community policing, or addressing some of the underlying issues that drive crime in the first place. It doesn't feel like we've got it figured out yet.

**(A) too little**

Drug addiction affects so many families and communities, and it seems like the response has often been more focused on punishment than on treatment and prevention. Recovery programs, mental health support, and community resources are chronically underfunded. When I look at the scale of the problem — overdose deaths, broken families, people cycling in and out of the justice system — it really feels like we're not investing nearly enough in actually solving it.

**(A) too little**

Honestly, education feels chronically underfunded to me. Teachers are still paying out of pocket for basic classroom supplies, school infrastructure in a lot of areas is crumbling, and we keep hearing about teacher shortages because the pay just isn't competitive enough to attract and retain good people. Whatever we're spending now, it doesn't seem to be enough to actually fix those problems.

**(A) too little**

Honestly, it feels like environmental issues keep getting pushed aside for more immediate concerns, but the long-term costs of not addressing them seem way higher than what we'd spend now. I see things like water quality issues, air pollution in cities, and extreme weather events getting worse, and it makes me think we're not investing nearly enough to get ahead of these problems. Penny-wise, pound-foolish, as they say.

**(C) too much**

Honestly, I think we're spending too much on welfare. It's not that I don't care about people who are struggling — I do — but it feels like the programs have grown really large and I'm not always sure they're helping people get back on their feet. Sometimes it seems like it creates dependency rather than opportunity. I'd rather see money going toward things like job training or education that help people become self-sufficient in the long run.

**(A) too little**

Honestly, it feels like we're always playing catch-up with healthcare. Between the cost of medications, access issues in rural areas, and mental health being underfunded for years — it doesn't seem like enough is being done. I know it's expensive, but the consequences of *not* investing show up in worse outcomes and higher long-term costs anyway.

**(A) too little**

There are still significant gaps in wealth, health outcomes, education, and criminal justice that haven't been adequately addressed. Incremental efforts haven't been enough to close those gaps in any meaningful way.

**(A) too little**

Honestly, I think we underfund space exploration. The long-term benefits — scientific discovery, technology spinoffs, planetary defense, and eventually expanding humanity's presence beyond Earth — seem worth a stronger investment. The actual NASA budget is a pretty small slice of federal spending, so the "we can't afford it" argument has always felt a bit overstated to me. Though I get why people prioritize more immediate problems here at home.

**(D) independent (neither, no response)**

I tend to look at issues and candidates individually rather than aligning strongly with either major party. Both parties have things I agree and disagree with, so "independent" feels most honest.

**(D) moderate, middle of the road**

I find myself agreeing with different sides on different issues — it really depends on the topic. I don't feel like I fit neatly into one end of the spectrum.

**(B) there should be laws against the distribution of pornography to persons under 18**

That feels like the right balance to me. Adults should generally be free to make their own choices about what they consume, but kids need protection — their brains are still developing and they shouldn't have easy access to that kind of content. Blanket bans on adults seem overly restrictive, but having no protections at all for minors goes too far the other way.
raw_responses.selected_option: there should be laws against the distribution of pornography to persons under 18

raw_responses.raw_text:
**(C) don't know**

Honestly, it's one of those questions I go back and forth on. There's no way to really know for certain, and I find I can't fully commit to either a confident yes or a definitive no. I'm genuinely uncertain.

**(A) approve**

I think the separation of church and state is an important principle. Public schools serve kids from all kinds of backgrounds and faiths — or no faith at all — and it wouldn't feel right to have a government institution leading religious practices. People can pray and read the Bible on their own time; that's a personal and family matter. The ruling seems fair to me.

**(D) not wrong at all**

As long as it's between consenting adults, I don't think there's anything wrong with it. People have the right to make their own choices about their relationships and personal lives.

**(B) second law**

People shouldn't be turned away from buying a home just because of their race. That kind of discrimination causes real harm and keeps communities unfairly divided. The second law is the right call.

**(B) more or less satisfied**

Things are generally okay — bills get paid, there's food on the table — but there's always that feeling that a little more cushion would go a long way. Not complaining, but not exactly comfortable either.

**(A) favor**

Sex education in public schools makes sense to me. Kids are going to encounter this information one way or another — better they get accurate, age-appropriate information from educators than from unreliable sources. It helps with health, safety, and making informed decisions. I'd rather young people be informed than left in the dark.

(C) disagree

I think there are always better ways to discipline a child — setting clear boundaries, consistent consequences, time-outs, having a real conversation. Physical discipline might feel like it "works" in the moment, but the research pretty consistently shows it doesn't lead to better long-term outcomes and can actually cause harm to the relationship and the child's development. So I can't say it's ever *necessary*.

**(A) Yes, allowed to speak**

Free speech is pretty fundamental. Even if someone's views are unpopular or offensive to many people in the community, they should still have the right to express them publicly. That's kind of the whole point — protecting speech that not everyone agrees with. I might personally disagree with their message, but silencing them isn't the answer.

**(A) Yes, allowed to speak.**

Free speech is free speech. I might completely disagree with his views, but if we start deciding who gets to speak based on their political beliefs, that's a slippery slope. The answer to speech you disagree with is more speech, not silence. Let him talk — people can make up their own minds.

**(A) Yes, allowed to speak**

My reasoning: I find those views repugnant and scientifically false, but I believe in free speech even for ideas I strongly disagree with. Suppressing speech — even hateful speech — sets a dangerous precedent about who gets to decide what ideas are permissible. The better response is to counter bad ideas with better ones, not silence.

**(A) yes**

If someone is facing an incurable disease with no hope of recovery — especially if they're suffering — I think they should have the right to make that decision for themselves. It's about autonomy and dignity. Forcing someone to endure prolonged suffering against their will doesn't seem right to me.

**(A) too high**

Honestly, when I look at my paycheck and see what gets taken out, it's hard not to feel like it's a lot. I understand taxes fund important things, but the amount just feels like more than it should be for what I personally get back from it day-to-day.

**(B) can't be too careful**

Honestly, I think caution is just the realistic approach. It's not that I think most people are *bad* — most people are probably fine — but "trust" is something that should be earned over time rather than assumed upfront. You don't really know someone's motivations until you've had some experience with them. I'd rather start cautious and be pleasantly surprised than assume the best and get burned.

**(D) disagree somewhat**

The comparison feels off to me. The experiences of Irish or Italian immigrants, while genuinely difficult, were different in kind and scale from what Black Americans faced — centuries of slavery, then legally enforced segregation, then systemic barriers that persisted well into living memory. Those other groups faced discrimination, yes, but they weren't legally *property* and weren't systematically prevented from building wealth for generations.

I also bristle a bit at the framing of "special favors" — policies aimed at addressing documented, structural disadvantages don't feel like favors to me, more like corrections.

That said, I stop short of "disagree strongly" because I do think there's something genuine in the underlying value of self-determination and community resilience, and I recognize people hold this view in good faith.

**(A) Always wrong**

Marriage is a commitment, and breaking that trust through infidelity causes real harm — to the partner, the relationship, and often families involved. I don't see circumstances that justify it.

If a man and a woman have sexual relations before marriage, do you think it is always wrong, almost always wrong, wrong only sometimes, or not wrong at all?
